beats.narration_text: Hello, this is Liam, in for Bear. The ask: how can a chatbot answer questions about my own documents, when it has never read them? Show me how RAG works, step by step.

show.event: composer card fades in on cream
greeting 'Hello, Liam' types above the composer

props.command: How can a chatbot answer questions about my own documents, when it has never read them? Show me how RAG works, step by step.
output: the idea: look things up first, then write the answer
worked example: a shop handbook, a laptop return, 30 days
where it breaks: an old page in the store wins the search

beats.role_note: COLD OPEN LAW — ask lands answered; Liam introduced in first breath.

beats.narration_text: With RAG, a chatbot answers from what it just looked up. It searches your documents for the closest pieces, pastes them into the prompt, and writes from them. RAG stands for retrieval-augmented generation.

show.event: types 'With RAG, a chatbot answers\nfrom what it memorized.'
'from what it memorized' turns terracotta, hesitates, backspaces
types 'from what it just looked up'

beats.role_note: EXECUTIVE-SUMMARY LAW — misconception corrected: the model does not memorize your files; it retrieves the relevant pieces at question time.

beats.narration_text: Start with a box of your own documents. Here, it's a small shop's handbook. The model never saw these pages in training, so on its own, it can only guess what they say.

shot.visual_intent: A taped kraft box drops onto the stage and lands with a floor shadow; 'handbook' beside it. A faint dashed thought-line from a dark model block at right stops short of the box, ending in a small grey '?' tick.

beats.narration_text: Open the box, and there are three documents: returns, shipping, and warranty. RAG doesn't teach the model these pages. It hands the model the right page, at the moment it answers.

beats.narration_text: Step one: cut every document into chunks, short pieces the system can fetch one at a time. Each of these documents has two sentences, so each becomes two chunks. Six chunks in all.

shot.visual_intent: A terracotta cut line sweeps across each page in turn; each page separates into two paper slips; the six slips settle in a row; '6 chunks' beside them.

beats.narration_text: Step two: turn each chunk into an embedding, a list of numbers. Our toy version counts words, with one slot for each of the handbook's twenty-nine key words. Real systems use a trained model, so chunks that mean the same thing land close together.

shot.visual_intent: The slips ride a conveyor through a checkpoint scanner; a scan line sweeps each; each slip exits trailing a strip of grey bars of different heights (its embedding). '29 numbers' beside the strips.

beats.narration_text: Step three: file every embedding in a vector store, a database built to find the closest lists of numbers, fast. This happens once, ahead of time, before anyone asks a thing.

beats.narration_text: Now a question arrives. How long do I have to return a laptop? It goes through the same scanner, so it becomes a list of numbers too, in the same space as the chunks.

beats.narration_text: Step four: the store compares the question's numbers with every chunk's, and returns the closest. The returns chunk scores zero point five eight. The warranty chunk shares only the word laptop, so it scores zero point two five. The other four share no words, and score zero.

beats.narration_text: Step five: paste the top two chunks into the prompt, above the question, with one instruction: answer only from these notes, and say so if they don't cover it. Now the facts sit right in front of the model.

beats.narration_text: The model reads the prompt and writes a grounded answer: thirty days, from the returns chunk. Because you know which chunks went in, the answer can point back to its source, and you can check it.

beats.narration_text: Here's where it fails. Same question, but someone has added an old FAQ page that says fourteen days. It repeats the question almost word for word, so it now scores zero point six eight, and the right chunk drops to second, at zero point three eight.
beats.motion_claim: The tab pill slides from Before to After; the ranking is replaced, and the stale FAQ chunk now sits on top.
beats.why_card: Card test: (1) the idea is two sets of real executed scores; (2) the tab switch flipping the ranking IS 'one added page changes what ranks first'; (3) the drawers cannot show two rankings side by side with numbers.

beats.narration_text: Now the prompt leads with the old chunk. A model told to trust its notes can answer fourteen days, fluently and confidently. Nothing in the writing looks wrong. The mistake happened earlier, at retrieval.

shot.visual_intent: An old, dog-eared page drops into the box; its slip rides the scanner into a drawer; that drawer opens, the slip lands on top of the prompt sheet; the model pushes out an answer card '14 days'; the thread runs back to the old slip, and a terracotta ring circles that drawer. beats.narration_text: That's the idea behind RAG. In the 2020 paper that named it, Lewis and colleagues gave a model twenty-one million Wikipedia passages to search, and updated what the model knew by swapping in a newer copy of Wikipedia.

shot.visual_intent: The one drawer cabinet multiplies into a long wall of grey cabinets receding in isometric rows; a counter climbs to '21M'; caption 'per Lewis et al. 2020'; one cabinet slides out and a newer one slides in.

beats.narration_text: Let's recap with Claude. Cut your documents into chunks, and turn each chunk into an embedding, a list of numbers. File them in a vector store. When a question arrives, embed it too, and fetch the closest chunks. Paste them into the prompt, and the model answers from them. And if the store holds an old page, the answer goes old with it. Fix the store, not the model.

props.artifactHeading: How RAG works, in six lines
artifactLines: Cut your documents into chunks; embed each one as a list of numbers.
File the embeddings in a vector store.
Embed the question and fetch the closest chunks.
Paste them into the prompt; the model answers from them.
A stale page in the store gives a stale answer: fix the store.
The 2020 paper that named it searched 21 million Wikipedia passages.

beats.role_note: VERDICT page — the recap the show-tell cut lacked; restates the body, no new claims.

beats.narration_text: Your turn. Paste this into Claude: Here are three short passages from my own notes: [paste them]. And here is my question: [your question]. Before you answer, rank the passages by how relevant each one is to the question, and say why. Then answer using only the top passage, and quote the sentence you used. Then check two things yourself. Does the quoted sentence really say the answer? And would a newer passage say something different? If it would, the retrieval picked wrong.

props.command: Here are three short passages from my own notes: [paste them]. And here is my question: [your question]. Before you answer, rank the passages by how relevant each one is to the question, and say why. Then answer using only the top passage, and quote the sentence you used.
output: Check: the quoted sentence really says the answer.
Check: no newer passage would change it.

rubric: The quoted sentence states the answer itself, not something near it.
No newer or more specific passage in your notes contradicts it; if one does, retrieval picked wrong.
